The internet of "things"

By: Sasha Schwendenwein | Delivery

Proposal


Show: Carte Blanche

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
Your car, your house and even your pace maker may be susceptible to hacking as they are all NOW connected to the internet.

Unique Selling Point:
We will go to an online house with an expert and will be shown how the "things" in it will...Same people as password story, but obviously on the "internet of things." These are all the "things" that are now connected to the internet and making sure our audience is aware of their connection and the worst case scenario of what may happen.

We will find a case study - and scare them regarding everything that is online... so their car could be hacked through bluetooth, their home thermostat could be held for ransom, and the newest hackable target for hackers who want a ransom are medical implants - like pace makers. We have real world examples of all of these things and we are going to bring it home to South Africa by interviewing a south african whose house is online.

I think it could be a great 5-6 minute story on the threats that this poses.

NOTES FROM BRON: "The internet of things is not only about hacking. We will need to include, the pros and the cons as well as the what this means for advertising in your homes, push notifications, in-appliance purchases that could come with your home being online and such connectivity abused.
What about knowing your movements throughout the home (sensors) and when you’re out.
How does this impact on privacy as well?

We’ll need to touch on further applications like intelligent transport, smart grids and smart cities – with overseas EGs (or African if there are). Experts estimate that the IoT will consist of almost 50 billion objects by 2020. What are the possibilities – what’s next and where are we on this timeline?

I know you already have your car, thermostat and pacemaker egs, but let’s keep this in mind:

"Things," in the IoT sense, can refer to a wide variety of devices such as heart monitoring implants, biochip transponders on farm animals, electric clams in coastal waters, automobiles with built-in sensors, DNA analysis devices for environmental/food/pathogen monitoring or field operation devices that assist firefighters in search and rescue operations. Legal scholars suggest to look at "Things" as an "inextricable mixture of hardware, software, data and service". These devices collect useful data with the help of various existing technologies and then autonomously flow the data between other devices. Current market examples include smart thermostat systems and washer/dryers that use Wi-Fi for remote monitoring.
As well as the expansion of Internet-connected automation into a plethora of new application areas, IoT is also expected to generate large amounts of data from diverse locations, with the consequent necessity for quick aggregation of the data, and an increase in the need to index, store, and process such data more effectively."



Summary:
Keitumetsi - spoke about how hackers work with ransomeware and the fact that soon we will need our own security people - like chubb for online etc she also speak about how hackers work - black and white hat, ransomware

Evan speaks about the car example, the thermostat example and others.

Rika Butler said the number one danger for 2016 is medical implants being hacked like your pacemaker. I can script her, if you think it's similar to use all of the experts from previous story.

Press Release:


The Internet of Things
Our physical world is fast becoming a single, great interconnected information system. From smart phones to smart cars and smart cities, the possibilities seem limitless. Carte Blanche asks: what sort of risks are we facing in a world controlled by devices that increasingly monitor and connect our every move?



Script:


Imagine a home where the lights, climate control, entertainment and security speak to each other. With all of these and other devices in digital synchrony to enhance life, does a house become more than just a home?
LINK: “PRETTY SOON YOUR WHOLE LIFE WILL BE ONLINE, BY 2020, 50 BILLION THINGS WILL HAVE INTERNET CONNECTION. WHAT IS THE IOT OR THE “INTERNET OF THINGS”?
Bartho Erusmas: “Well the internet of things basically refers to a whole lot of devices that have been connected together, all sharing data amongst each other.
Bartho Erusmas is a Home Automation specialist who made this a “smart home.”
Claire: “So machines talking to machines?”
Bartho: “You could say that yet, it’s not like Skynet terminator, but they’re more sharing data.”
Nnamdi Oranye wrote the book on using tech innovation in Africa, he says the internet of things includes sensors on manual devices that provide key data.
Oranye: “You have smart cement in the road to tell you that it/s raining, and it can talk to the car to slow down. that’s the basics of the internet of things.
Another example are Uber’s driverless vehicles in America.
Oranye: “You know we struggle with things like traffic congestion, so with driverless cars that talk to each other the traffic congestion sort of becomes easier.”
Bartho ensures data is optimally used to create a smart-living environment, like with climate control.
Bartho: “Just switch on the air-conditioning or the heating system lets say 5.30 in the morning, by the time you escape from underneath the covers, the room is already the desired temperature.”
South Africa is actually among the top 10 countries applying the IOT to daily life.
LINK: “THE OBVIOUS ADVANTAGES OF BECOMING MORE CONNECTED IS THAT YOU ELIMINATE MENIAL TASKS IN THE HOME, YOU BECOME MORE ENERGY EFFICIENT AND YOU CAN TAKE CONTROL OF ALL YOUR SECURITY, ALL AT THE TOUCH OF A BUTTON.”
However, your home may become more susceptible to being hacked.
Bartho: “I mean for remote access here, there’s multiple encryption that’s on it, the hosting gets done overseas, but the big thing is, why would they necessarily want to hack your home? To put your lights off while you’re cooking.”
Oranye: “What you need to consider, however, is as you apply more technologies into a connected home, your points of entry will increase.”
Claire: “I think we need to start thinking differently about security.”
Oranye: “Cyber security exists now, with any technology in play, so you need to apply the same logic of securing your entire ecosystem.”
Is the idea of hackers holding your life to ransom already a reality?
Nnamdi Oranye: “If I use an example of malware with the pacemakers, someone could hack into your pacemaker, and then force you to provide some ransom in that regard.”
In this experiment featured on wired.com two hackers proved that they could stop a vehicle in its tracks.
Hackers: “So were killing the engine right now.”
Car slows.
There are also concerns around privacy. Could your every move be tracked?
Namadi: “With any new technology we have to invest so that its safe, secure and reliable, but we need to put a framework around it to make sure it’s only used for certain activities.”
We can use this technology to monitor our loved ones, or even our health and what we eat.
Bartho: “your system can actually monitor the contents of your refrigerator, and say that milk is on the verge of going sour.”
Claire: “We live in the future, we are the jetsons.”
Bartho: “your fridge can run advertisements or on its shopping list that It’s planning for you, that maybe you must you get these 2% low-fat yogurts.”
Nnamdi Oranye: “We have to take a needs based approach, healthcare, stock to remote areas in Africa or south Africa when they’ve run out.”
The IOT has opened a digital Pandora’s box. And as implantable micro-chips become more mainstream, humans could also be connected 24.7.


PROMO 1: 10 SECONDER
IT’S CALLED THE INTERNET OF THINGS - A WORLD IN WHICH EVERY ITEM WE OWN OR USE – FROM HOMES TO CARS – IS DIGITALLY CONNECTED TO EVERYTHING ELSE. BUT WHAT ARE THE RISKS?

PROMO 2: 15 SECONDER
Oranye: “What you need to consider, however, is as you apply more technologies into a connected home, your points of entry will increase.”
WHAT RISKS ARE YOU FACING IN A WORLD GOVERNED BY THE SO-CALLED INTERNET OF THINGS – SMART DEVICES THAT MONITOR YOUR EVERY MOVE?

PROMO 3: 15 SECONDER
THE INTERNET OF THINGS, HOW IS THE INFINITE NETWORK BETWEEN MACHINES AND DEVICES MAKING OUR LIVES “SMART”?

Bartho: “your system can actually monitor the contents of your refrigerator, 7.21 and say that milk is on the verge of going sour.”
